James I. King of England and Ireland from 1603 to 1625, having already ruled Scotland as James VI since 1567. The first Stuart monarch of England, he succeeded Elizabeth I and unified the crowns of England, Scotland, and Ireland for the first time. His reign saw the beginning of English colonization of the Americas, but was also marked by theological conflicts and disputes with Parliament that would foreshadow greater upheavals to come.

James was the target of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, a Catholic conspiracy led by Robert Catesby and Guy Fawkes to blow up the House of Lords in an attempt to assassinate him. The plot's discovery became a defining moment of his reign, celebrated annually in Britain. He was also a patron of literature and religious scholarship. James commissioned the King James Version of the Bible, which was published in 1611 and became a cornerstone of English literature and liturgy, influencing English prose for centuries to come.

He was the first monarch to call himself the King of Great Britain, attempting to politically unify England and Scotland on the level of formal titles. Beyond governance, James was an intellectual monarch who authored Daemonologie, a treatise on witchcraft and demonology, and Basilikon Doron, a book of instructions for his son on the nature of kingship. His reign saw the establishment of Jamestown in 1607, the first permanent English settlement in the Americas. Elizabeth I had executed his mother, Mary, Queen of Scots, but named him her successor. His son Charles I would inherit the throne and face the English Civil War that would define the seventeenth century.
